fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "God as a Verb, Truth as Reality", "body": "Chance opens by proposing that once truth is defined as reality itself, nobody needs to go seeking it, because what exists is the truth. Clint builds on that through grammar. He argues the legal system runs on nouns, names and titles, which are empty forms, while verbs and adjectives stay closer to the truth. He notes that \"the truth will set you free\" is a Bible verse most people quote without knowing it, reads God in the old sense of a magistrate or anyone holding power over you, and says Webster's 1828 treats Jehovah as a verb, so creation is something always happening rather than a past event."}, {"title": "Rock, Paper, Scissors as an Order of Needs", "body": "Clint offers rock, paper and scissors as a ranking of human priorities. The rock is need, the foundation and the truth. The scissors are ease, a tool like a plow, and also the intellect, which cuts and categorizes. The paper is want and desire, a thin covering like a noun, and in a materialist world he says it has covered the rock. Chance notes the paper is two dimensional against a three dimensional rock and casts the scissors as the reason that can separate fiction from reality. Clint answers that the same tool can lead to sin, a word he links to synthetic and to words carrying the prefix dis."}, {"title": "Simulators, Copies and the Replaced Axe", "body": "Clint says the original script of The Matrix made it a voluntary virtual reality people chose and then lost the will to leave. Clint argues that in the old dictionaries simulation means hypocrisy, knowing the moral law and acting against it, while a simulacrum is a copy without an original. Chance recalls an example from Clint's own show, an axe whose head and then handle are both replaced. Clint carries it into transhumanism, asking whether a person rebuilt from new parts is the same, and says change is part of life and worth embracing. In his outro Chance points to Cyberpunk 2077 as that transhuman future."}, {"title": "Why Freedom Means Self-Responsibility", "body": "Clint describes church and state as a mutual pardon, the priest class forgiving the politicians and the politicians forgiving the priests, and cites maxims of law holding that the king can break no law. Chance says this is why he is not chasing researchers who promise ways to game the legal system. Clint argues most slaves would not have chosen freedom because the plantation felt safe, and reads offers of hope, safety and security as the sign of coming tyranny. Freedom, in his telling, is self-responsibility, including self-sustainability, which he doubts anyone manages alone. He adds that insurance still recognizes acts of God, and that legal freedom really means franchise."}, {"title": "Time as the Currency of the Legal System", "body": "Clint argues that legal equality means everyone is equally punishable, so a poor man pays for a crime with jail time while the rich and corporations pay fines, because time is money and money is time. He asks whether a contract or a mortgage could bind anyone without a due date, suggests a good job is one you would keep doing without pay, and calls time one of the four corners of the fiction. Chance adds that debt-based money works like musical chairs. In his outro he explains Clint's cartoon metaphor: a life logged as timestamped transactions, frame by frame, looks alive to an algorithm."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Author, researcher and documentary maker Clint Richardson returns to help us find clarity on what is real and what is artificial. We explore occult language dynamics, the gods vs. God, Simulation & Simulacra, our choices with the legal realm, what what the phrase "time is money" is really saying.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title":"For and Against as One Machine","body":"Early in the members' hour Chance asks how being for something can prop it up, and Richardson points to the Webster's 1828 entry where for is defined as against. He argues the two major parties are special interests that should have no place in politics, two hands of the same body, so opposing one simply strengthens the other. He compares the pairing to the Church of England as Catholic Lite, invokes Lenin's useful idiot, and says nature itself holds no for or against, only existence and the consequences of our own actions."},{"title":"Voting, Electors and the Right to Say No","body":"Richardson argues that the popular vote is theater, that the Electoral College actually chooses the president, and that an elector is a master while a voter is a slave. In his view casting a ballot surrenders the one power that matters, the power to say no, which is why he notes the movement to add none of the above. He calls the president the CEO of a corporation and Congress its board, insisting even Gandhi would have to run the fiction. Chance adds that enfranchisement works like buying a McDonald's franchise inside nesting corporate dolls."},{"title":"Bloodlines, Heraldry and the Meaning of Race","body":"Richardson claims presidents and senators trace to the same families, citing George Bush and John Kerry as eighth cousins once removed. He reads the right to bear Arms as a right to display family heraldry rather than weapons, and argues race originally meant family, so the true racism is nepotism among ruling bloodlines while the public is divided by skin color. He warns against handing DNA to genealogy companies. Chance raises consanguinity from Richardson's book and the fabled genealogies of rulers, a phrase Richardson credits to the Bible, and Richardson adds that the maxims of law hold that relation can never truly be proven."},{"title":"Names, Titles and the Invisible Spoon","body":"Richardson argues that a license is permission to do what the law otherwise forbids, and says anarchy has been turned into a meme and a product, since the self-described anarchist still shows a driver's license in court. Chance admits he wore that title for a couple of years and now sees why no title is safer. Richardson reads the spoon scene in The Matrix as a lesson that the object is real but the name is not, extends it to property titles and to terms like woman and human, and says no one can know a legal library that could fill a house and changes with a single word."},{"title":"Leaving the Matrix Without Leaving Nature","body":"The closing stretch asks how anyone actually leaves the system. Richardson insists nobody ever left nature, that the fight is a spiritual war with the principalities, and that the truth movement has become an artificial womb of shared inaction. He uses an ant colony removing a cordyceps-infected ant as his picture of protection, argues that birth certificates and continued use of a name amount to consent, and admits he has no clean answer beyond forming a religious society. Chance shares his own first step, recalling Richardson's test that any job you would not do as charity may not be worth doing."}]
